segments.text: You do not need a website, a logo, or a hundred followers to get
your first freelance client.
You need one clear offer.
Today I will show you the exact three steps I recommend: define the offer,
tell people you know, and send a few honest pitches.
Step one: write down one thing you can do for one kind of client,
in one sentence you could say out loud.
For example: I write welcome emails for online shops, or I tidy messy spreadsheets
for small clinics.
If you cannot say it in one sentence, narrow it down.
A narrow offer is easier to buy than a long list of skills.
Step two: tell twenty people you already know that you are taking on one
small project this month.
Friends, former colleagues, cousins, neighbours: in my experience, a first client often comes from
someone you already know, not from strangers.
Keep it short and human.
Say what you do, who it is for, and that you have room for
one project.
Step three: send five personal pitches to businesses you genuinely like, one per day
for a week.
Read their website first, mention one specific thing you noticed, and suggest one small
job you could do next week.
Most people will not reply, and that is normal.
Silence usually means busy, not rude, so keep your routine going.
If someone replies with interest, answer within a day, suggest a short call, and
send a simple written quote after it.
Agree the scope, the deadline and the price in writing before you start, even
if it is just a plain email.
Do the work carefully, deliver a day early if you can, and ask for
a short testimonial when the client is happy.
One project done well beats ten half-finished ones, because that first testimonial makes the
second client much easier.
If you want my exact pitch template, join the free newsletter at freelance dot
example slash first-client.
See you next time.
